r: Every recursive resolver keeps copies of the answers it receives. Each record carries a TTL, a 32-bit counter of seconds defined in RFC 1035, which lets the resolver reuse the answer without asking the authoritative server again. Suppose you change an A record at noon and its TTL is 3600 seconds. A resolver that queried it at 11:59 will keep handing out the old IP address until nearly 1 p.m., and clients will assume that address is current because nothing tells them otherwise. So the cache expiry window on the resolver, not your edit, determines how fast the change spreads. Negative answers are cached too. Under RFC 2308, a resolver that cached NXDOMAIN before your new subdomain existed will keep saying it doesn't exist until the SOA minimum runs out. Browsers and OS stub resolvers add their own caches, and some ignore TTLs entirely. I call this TTL debt. Operators should lower TTLs to 300 seconds one full old-TTL period before a migration, or the internet will keep navigating by an outdated map.
